Verse Engine 2.0 — release notes for humans#

Verse Engine 2.0 is out, and the changelog is long. This is the short version, written for the people who will use Verse rather than build it: what you can do now, what changed if you were already using it, and what is still marked "beta".

In one paragraph#

Verse turns a heavy 3D model or scan into a link. Open the link and the space streams in — first a soft version of the whole thing in a few seconds, then detail wherever you look — in current browsers, on laptops and phones, with no app to install. 2.0 is the first release we call production: it is deployed, and its speed and colour accuracy are measured by automated tests.

What you can do now#

Share a space with a link. Upload a .glb (or a scan) in the playground, wait for the compile — a minute or two for a product, about twenty minutes for a building — and copy the share link. Anyone can open it in a current browser. The file is digitally signed, and the viewer shows "signed" once it has verified it.

Keep it private. Sign in (the account is a token, like an API key), flip a scene to private, and mint a share token per person. Each token is a separate key you can revoke later without touching the others. Strangers see nothing — not even that the scene exists.

Collect comments inside the space. Every share link doubles as a review round. Your client clicks any spot and types a note; it is pinned to that exact 3D position and everyone who opens the link sees the numbered pin. You resolve or delete pins as the owner. No client account needed.

Export a video. One click records a flythrough — the automatic ~30 s tour the compiler lays out, or one you recorded — to a 1080p MP4 or WebM, inside the viewer's own browser. Nothing is uploaded.

Walk through it. Press Walk: real walls block you, stairs work, the floor-plan minimap shows where you are. Measure a distance in two clicks. Or tour together live, as avatars, with follow mode.

Put it on your own website. One script tag embeds the viewer; your page needs no special headers or build step, and the embed reports events (ready, loaded, progress, picks, dwell time) your page can act on.

Publish from your tools. Blender has a one-click Publish to Verse panel, verified end to end. Unity and Unreal exporters exist and speak the same protocol; they are marked beta until their first in-editor runs. (Update, 4.0: the Unity and Unreal plug-ins have since been verified in the real editors — Unity 6000.6.5f1 and Unreal Engine 5.8.3 — and are no longer beta.)

What changed if you were already using Verse#

  • The viewer defaults to on-demand rendering in embeds: a still scene costs essentially no battery. The playground still renders continuously.
  • HDR display output is on automatically on HDR-capable screens for the top device tier. Add ?hdr=0 to any link destined for an SDR screen or a video export.
  • Share links never break. Every URL ever issued (/?vpk=…, ?experience=, ?tour=) keeps serving the app; the bare domain now shows the product page, and /app is the playground.
  • Compiles are faster since 2.0.1: about 1.8× on large scenes, with byte-identical output. If you run your own server, budget about 8 GB of memory for ingest; the two compile phases now genuinely overlap.
  • Errors are honest. Every error the app itself returns carries an X-Verse-Error: 1 header and a JSON message, so you can always tell an app error from a network hiccup.

What is still beta#

  • Unity and Unreal publishing. Protocol-tested against a live server; the first in-editor smoke test is pending. The Blender add-on is the reference. (Update, 4.0: the Unity and Unreal plug-ins have since been verified in the real editors — Unity 6000.6.5f1 and Unreal Engine 5.8.3 — and are no longer beta.)
  • Gaussian splats stream, but the walk-through, review and video tooling is still mesh-first.
  • The WebGL2 fallback (older browsers, some in-app browsers) streams the same scenes since 2.1, without post effects. Gaussian splats still need WebGPU. (Update, 4.0: the WebGL2 build now gets the studio lighting, shadows, bloom, optional ambient occlusion, reflection probes and real-time GI too.)
  • Headsets. The WebXR mode is experimental and has not yet been verified on a physical headset.
  • Materials. Vertex colours, texture transforms and the KHR_materials_* extensions (clearcoat, transmission, sheen and similar) are not rendered yet.

Where to read more#

  • The changelog — every change, newest first; updated with each release.
  • How Verse streams a 3-million-triangle building into your browser in seconds — the idea behind all of this, explained with diagrams.
  • The getting-started guide — five minutes from a file to a link.
